drainage.local_h: Following Gladewater runoff back to where it starts
local: On bigger Gladewater properties the wet spot is rarely where the problem begins. Water arrives from upslope: a neighbor's field, a road ditch, or a long drive that funnels runoff toward the house. If we only dig where it is soggy, the next rain brings it back. So we walk the whole property, during or right after a rain when we can, and trace the water from where it enters to where it sits.

The soil explains a lot. Gladewater ground is sandy on top with clay below. Rain soaks the sand quickly, hits the clay and stops, and after that the water either pools in low spots or moves sideways toward the foundation. Heavy rain in long stretches makes it worse. The expensive part of any drainage job is the digging, so we would rather build it correctly once than see it silt up in a season.

Fixes range from small to large. A downspout extension or reroute handles roof water. Regrading and a swale can move surface water across a lawn. A French drain, with sock-wrapped pipe in #57 stone, picks up water under the surface. Where an outlet is needed, we use a catch basin, a pop-up emitter, a lower part of the lot or daylight. A standard single run is $1,900 to $3,000, and full systems run $3,000 to $4,500.

On larger lots we combine fixes across the whole slope, and large or combined projects run $4,500 and up. We finish the trench with soil and sod, or rock or a dry creek bed if you prefer. Drainage goes in year-round, and digging is faster in a dry stretch when the clay is not saturated. Getting it done before spring rains means one less season with a pond in the yard.

faq.q: Can you handle drainage across a whole Gladewater property?
faq.a: Yes. On larger lots we look at the whole slope instead of only the wet corner, and may combine swales, regrading and French drains. Full systems usually run $3,000 to $4,500, and large properties can go higher. The estimate is written and itemized.

faq.q: Why does my yard stay wet after rain?

faq.q: Where does the water go once you install a drain?
faq.a: To a real outlet. That can be daylight, a lower part of your lot, a catch basin or a pop-up emitter. A drain with no outlet just fills up and fails. We dig with a steady fall toward the outlet and backfill with stone so clay fines cannot clog the pipe.

faq.q: When should I fix a drainage problem?
faq.a: Any time of year, but the best time to see the problem is during or right after a rain. Digging is quicker in a dry stretch. If you act before spring rains, you do not spend another season with standing water in the back corner.

fertilization.local_h: Feeding a lawn on Gladewater's sand over clay
local: Gladewater lawns sit on sandy loam over clay, and the sandy top layer is the problem with fertilizer. Nutrients move through it fast, especially after a long rain, so one heavy shot in spring mostly ends up in the ditch. That is why we spread the feeding across the season in slow-release applications. Each one goes down in a window when the grass can actually use it, and the plan is built on a soil sample from your lawn, not on the bag.

Pines are everywhere in the older parts of Gladewater, and years of needles and acidic rain pull soil pH down. The test tells us whether yours is low. When it is, we add lime to correct it, because grass cannot use fertilizer well in soil that is too acidic. Plenty of lawns we see are fed regularly and still thin out, and a pH problem is often the reason. We would rather fix the soil once than keep adding product on top of it.

Timing starts late. The first feeding goes down around April 25, once nighttime lows hold above 60 degrees and bermuda and St. Augustine are fully awake. Feeding in March mostly washes away. After that we come back in early July with a summer-safe feeding and in early September to build roots. The last real nitrogen goes down in September, because late nitrogen on St. Augustine feeds large patch when the nights turn cool.

October is a potassium month, with a winterizer for cold hardiness. On larger Gladewater properties the cost follows lawn size, which is why a visit starts from about $190 and bigger lawns are priced on their own. Where a lawn has packed down, we add core aeration between late August and mid-September, with the feeding right behind it. Compacted ground is common over clay. Bigger lawns simply take more product and more time, and the written plan shows both.

faq.q: When should I start fertilizing my Gladewater lawn?
faq.a: Not early. Wait until nighttime lows hold above 60 degrees, usually around late April. Feeding before the grass is growing mostly wastes product. We follow with feedings in early July and early September, then an October winterizer built around potassium, not nitrogen.

faq.q: Why do you test the soil before feeding?
faq.a: Because East Texas soil often runs a little acidic, and sandy ground like Gladewater's loses nutrients quickly. The test shows pH and what is missing, so the plan fits your lawn. If the pH is low, we add lime. Without a test, you are guessing at both.

faq.q: How much does fertilizing a Gladewater lawn cost?

faq.q: Do you treat weeds or insects in the lawn?
faq.a: No. We do not apply weed control or insect treatments. What we do is feed the lawn on a schedule, correct pH with lime, aerate packed ground and mow at the right height, which is what keeps a thick lawn crowding out thin spots on its own.

faq.q: Should I aerate my Gladewater lawn?
faq.a: If the ground has packed down, yes. Clay under a thin sandy layer compacts, and shallow roots are the result. We aerate between late August and mid-September and follow with the feeding. A quick walk over the lawn tells us whether it needs it that year.

flower-bed-installation.local_h: Planting beds that fit Gladewater's light and sandy soil
local: A flower bed in Gladewater lives or dies by the light. Beds under mature trees on the older streets deal with shade and roots competing for water, while a bed on open acreage bakes from morning to night. We count the hours of sun a bed gets at the walkthrough and choose plants for exactly that, rather than starting from a plant list and hoping the spot works. For full sun on open lots, lantana, salvia, Knock Out roses, daylilies and esperanza all take East Texas heat and keep blooming through July. In the shade, azaleas and hydrangeas work where they are sited out of the hot afternoon sun. Annuals like petunias and impatiens look great in April and are done by the Fourth, so we lean on tougher plants that need less babying. Tough, heat-loving plants also mean fewer replacements and less money spent each spring.

Gladewater soil is sandy loam over clay, which drains well until the top saturates and then holds water. We loosen the bed, work in compost, set the grade so water moves away from the house and plant with real spacing so air moves through the leaves. Wet feet kill more plants here than drought does, so we tell you to water deep and less often rather than a little every day.

Fall is the best time for shrubs and perennials, September through November, while the soil is still warm. Heat lovers like vinca wait until mid-May. Every bed finishes with mulch at 1 to 1.5 inches, pulled back off the stems. If you want to see the plan drawn first, our $199 Flower Bed Preview gives you a rendering, and a new bed is priced with the planting work. irrigation.local_h: Watering what matters on a large Gladewater property

The ground is sandy loam over red clay. The sand drinks fast and dries fast, then the clay stops the water and pushes it sideways. One long cycle floods the low corner and leaves the high side dry. mulch-installation.local_h: Why mulch goes fast on a wooded Gladewater lot

Depth is where most people go wrong. The online calculators say three inches, which is a number from snowier places. Here it sheds light rain, traps moisture against stems and trunks and gives voles cover to chew roots over the winter. We spread 1 to 1.5 inches, raked even, and taper it off at trunks and siding. Keep it a few inches away from your brick or siding. We never lay fabric under it.

Choice of material matters on a lot full of pines. Pine straw is available on request and suits the look of a pine-shaded yard, and we also spread hardwood, cypress, cedar and dyed black or brown mulch. retaining-walls.local_h: Holding back soil on Gladewater's slopes and banks
local: A retaining wall in Gladewater usually has one of two jobs. Either a yard slopes toward the house and needs a stepped wall to hold the soil and make level ground, or a drive has been cut into a bank and the bank needs support. Before we price anything, we measure the grade change, find where water comes from and work out what the wall has to hold. The written estimate then lists the material, height, length and drainage.

The ground matters here. Gladewater is sandy loam over clay, and the sand drinks water fast until the top saturates. Then the clay holds it, and that water pushes against whatever is in its way. Most failed walls in East Texas fail from water pressure, so we put a gravel chimney and a perforated drain pipe with an outlet behind every wall. That is how the wall survives a long wet stretch.

The base is the other half. Sandy soil over clay does not hold a wall set on undisturbed dirt. We excavate below grade, compact a crushed stone base and set the first course dead level, then build up with gravel backfill behind each course. On taller walls we add geogrid reinforcement, and if a wall is tall enough to need a stamped engineering plan, we tell you at the walkthrough.

We build segmental block, natural stone, boulder and timber walls, as well as short seating walls and terraces that step down a steep grade. If you live near Lake Gladewater, we build on the land side, not docks, boathouses or seawalls. A leaning wall should be looked at before the next wet season makes it worse, and we build year-round, with dry stretches best for digging. Terraced walls handle steeper grades by stepping the load down in smaller, safer stages.

faq.q: What is the difference between a garden wall and a structural wall?
faq.a: A garden wall is short and mostly shapes beds or levels a small area. A structural wall holds back a real load of soil, so it needs a deeper base, geogrid on taller builds and drainage behind it. Short garden walls start at a few thousand dollars, and tall structural walls can run $20,000 or more.

faq.q: How much does a retaining wall cost in Gladewater?

faq.q: Can you fix a leaning retaining wall?

sod-installation.local_h: Choosing and laying sod in Gladewater's mix of shade and open ground
local: Sun picks the grass, and Gladewater has both extremes. Older lots near downtown sit under tall pines and hardwoods, where bermuda thins to dirt by August no matter how it is fed. Some spots are too dark for any turf. If a patch under the trees gets under about four hours of sun, no sod will last there, and we will say so at the walkthrough. A shade bed or a mulched area does better and costs less to keep up. It is better to hear that before you pay for sod than after it turns brown in August. Under a pine canopy, mulch or a planted bed can give the area a finished look without fighting the shade.

The sandy topsoil here is why prep matters. We strip the old turf and weeds to bare soil, regrade, then till in two to three inches of compost or topsoil so the new roots have something to hold water. Sod goes down with staggered seams and no gaps, over starter fertilizer. Access for the pallets is one of the things we check, and a long drive or a tight gate on a Gladewater lot changes how we bring them in.

Sod is also how we finish drainage work. After a French drain or a regrade, the trench and any reshaped ground get covered in matching sod so it does not wash before it roots. Timing runs late April through August for bermuda and May through September for St. Augustine, which wants to be in by the end of September. New sod needs a deep morning soak every day for two weeks, and you get that schedule in writing.

faq.q: Can you sod over a spot you just drained in Gladewater?
faq.a: Yes. After a French drain or regrade, we put sod back over the trench and any reshaped ground so it does not wash out before it roots. Matching the existing grass keeps the repair from standing out. We can bundle both jobs into one written estimate.

faq.q: What grass should I put in a shady Gladewater yard?
faq.a: St. Augustine, usually Floratam, Palmetto or Raleigh depending on the shade level. Bermuda quits in shade and thins out by late summer. If the spot gets under about four hours of sun, no turf will thrive there for long, and a shade bed is the better option.

faq.q: How much does sod cost in Gladewater?
faq.a: Most projects run $1,500 to $4,700. Sod is priced by the pallet based on the square footage, so a small patch repair costs less, and a full-yard install with heavy prep costs more. Grass type, old turf removal and grading also change the number. You get it in writing.

faq.q: When is the best time to lay sod?
faq.a: Bermuda goes down best from late April through August, and St. Augustine from May through September. St. Augustine needs four to six weeks of root growth before dormancy, so get it in by the end of September. Sod laid in November sits on the ground like a rug.

faq.q: How do I water new sod?
faq.a: Deep, every morning, for the first two weeks, then taper to deeper, less frequent soaks once the roots take hold. We give you the schedule in writing. Skipping watering in July heat can brown out a new install in two weeks, so it is the part of the job that is up to you.

tree-planting.local_h: Getting a new tree through its first Gladewater summers
local: Around Gladewater, a lot of the open ground sits well away from any existing shade. A new tree planted there takes full sun from day one, with nothing to cool the soil and no neighbor tree breaking the wind. The first two summers decide whether it makes it. That shapes everything we do on those sites: tree choice, planting depth, a staked trunk if the wind is steady, and a plan for watering when the weather gets hot.

Species matters. Shumard oak and willow oak do well in this part of East Texas, and bald cypress handles wetter ground, which is useful in the low spots that hold water after a long rain. Pecans grow big and need plenty of room, so we do not put them near a house. We match the tree to the spot, the soil and what it will look like at full size, not just at planting.

The soil here is sandy on top with clay below, and a container tree arrives in a ball of light potting mix. Roots will not move easily between textures that different, so the ball can dry out in a day and a half in July while the clay nearby stays moist. We dig a wide, shallow hole, set the root flare at grade, cut circling roots and backfill with the native soil, then build a basin and a mulch ring held off the trunk.

Fall is the best window, from September until about Thanksgiving, because the soil stays warm after the air cools and roots keep growing for months. You get a written schedule that starts with deep soaks twice a week for the first six weeks, and on bigger installs we return around the 30-day mark to check that the tree is establishing. We also plant in spring, but those trees need more water through the summer.

faq.q: What shade trees grow well around Gladewater?
faq.a: Native oaks like Shumard and willow oak do well in this part of East Texas, and bald cypress handles wetter ground. Pecans work if there is plenty of room. We match the species to the spot, the soil and how big the tree will get, so it is not crowding your house in twenty years.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a tree here?
faq.a: Fall, from September until about Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm while the air cools, so roots grow for months before summer. A tree planted in October gets close to six months of root growth, versus about eight weeks for one planted in April. We plant year-round, but spring trees need more watering.

faq.q: How do you price tree planting?
faq.a: We do not publish a price, because the tree itself drives most of the cost. We walk the property, recommend a species and send a written quote that includes the aftercare plan. Size at planting, the number of trees, site access and soil and drainage at the spot all move the number.

faq.q: How often do I water a new tree?
faq.a: For a fall tree, soak the root ball twice a week for six weeks, weekly through November, then every ten to fourteen days in a dry winter. Use a hose on a trickle for about twenty minutes. Soak everything new the day before a hard freeze. We leave this in writing.

faq.q: Do you stake the trees you plant?
faq.a: Only when the site calls for it. On open, windy ground, a stake keeps the trunk from rocking while the roots take hold. In a sheltered spot, staking can do more harm than good. We decide at the walkthrough and tell you when the stakes can come off.

tree-shrub-care.local_h: Plants that outgrew their spots in Gladewater yards
local: Gladewater has plenty of established yards, and the plantings in them have had years to get too big. A crepe myrtle is pressing against a roofline. A holly has swallowed half a front walk. A small tree has leaned over a fence line to get out of the shade of a bigger one. We walk the property, identify each plant, and flag what should be pruned, what should be left alone and what is past saving.

Timing is by species. Crepe myrtles get thinned in February while they are dormant, and we thin them, we do not top them. Topped trees grow back taller on weaker wood, and recovery takes two or three winters. Azaleas wait until right after they bloom. Hollies and boxwoods go in early summer. Knock Out roses are cut back hard in the same February window as the crepe myrtles. Each species has its own window, so we keep the calendar and schedule your yard to it.

Oaks are a separate case. East Texas has oak wilt, and the beetles that spread it are drawn to fresh pruning wounds in spring and early summer, so we leave oaks alone then. Dead lower limbs on the shade trees can be cleared in the same visit. Large trees close to a house or a power line belong to a tree service or the utility. If we see signs of trouble on a tree, we tell you plainly and point you to the right person.

After a storm, we pick up downed limbs, trim broken ends back to clean cuts and haul it all away. We can also remove small trees and shrubs, refresh mulch around tree bases and feed trees and shrubs on a seasonal schedule. Because every yard is different, the quote is itemized from the walkthrough, with no flat price posted ahead of time. Many Gladewater yards need a mix of these jobs at once, so we bundle them into one visit and one quote.

faq.q: Do you clean up storm limbs in Gladewater?
faq.a: Yes. After a storm we pick up downed limbs and branches, trim broken ends back to clean cuts and haul it off. A large tree down on a house or a power line is a job for a tree service or the utility, not for us.

faq.q: When should I prune my crepe myrtles?
faq.a: In February, while they are dormant and before the buds break. We thin out crossing and crowded wood and keep the natural shape. We do not top them. If yours were topped before, we plan a recovery over two or three winters instead of fixing it in one cut.

faq.q: Can you take out a small tree or shrub that has died?
faq.a: Yes. Removal of small trees and shrubs is part of the service, along with hauling the debris off. For a large tree near the house or a power line, call a tree service. We will tell you at the walkthrough which side of that line your tree falls on.

faq.q: Why do you avoid pruning oaks in spring?
faq.a: Oak wilt is a fungus in East Texas, and beetles that spread it are most active in spring and early summer, drawn to fresh cuts. We prune oaks in winter or late summer instead. If a limb breaks in a storm and has to come off, we cut it clean right away.

faq.q: How do you price tree and shrub work?
faq.a: We do not publish a flat price because the work varies too much from yard to yard. After a free walkthrough you get an itemized quote in writing, usually within a day. It reflects the number of plants, their size and condition, any removal and how much debris we haul away.
